questions.q: Dengue fever, a viral disease common in Pakistan, is spread from person to person by:
questions.x: Dengue virus is carried by Aedes mosquitoes, mainly Aedes aegypti. Anopheles mosquitoes carry the malaria parasite, which is a protozoan, not a virus.

questions.q: Viruses are said to lie on the borderline of living and non-living. A feature that links them with living organisms is that they:
o: Have no metabolism of their own
questions.x: Having genetic material that is inherited and can mutate is a feature of life. Crystallisation and lack of metabolism are features of non-living things.

questions.q: An icosahedral (polyhedral) capsid is a solid made of:
questions.x: An icosahedron has 20 equilateral triangular faces and 12 corners. Many viruses, such as adenovirus and poliovirus, have this capsid shape.

questions.q: Bread dough rises when yeast is added and left in a warm place because the yeast:
o: Releases carbon dioxide by fermenting sugar
Produces lactic acid that expands the dough
questions.x: Yeast ferments sugars in the dough to ethanol and carbon dioxide. The gas forms bubbles that make the dough rise; the ethanol evaporates during baking.

questions.q: In respiration, the oxidation of a substrate molecule usually means:
o: Addition of carbon dioxide to it
Removal of hydrogen (with its electrons) from it
questions.x: Biological oxidation is mostly dehydrogenation: dehydrogenase enzymes remove hydrogen atoms and pass them to NAD+ or FAD. Gaining hydrogen is reduction.

questions.q: Cellulose chains are straight rather than coiled mainly because:
o: Each β-glucose unit is turned through 180° relative to the next one
Each α-glucose unit is joined by α(1→6) branches
The chains are held by peptide bonds
questions.x: In cellulose, β(1→4) links make alternate glucose units flip over, giving a straight chain. This lets chains lie side by side and form hydrogen-bonded fibres.

questions.q: Which polysaccharide does NOT give glucose on complete hydrolysis?
questions.x: Chitin is a polymer of N-acetylglucosamine, a nitrogen-containing sugar derivative. Starch, glycogen and cellulose are all polymers of glucose.

questions.q: Equal masses of water and ethanol at the same temperature receive the same amount of heat. Which result is expected?
o: The water warms less, because it has a higher specific heat
The water warms more, because it has a lower specific heat
Both warm by exactly the same amount
The water freezes while the ethanol warms
questions.x: Water needs more heat per gram to raise its temperature by 1 °C than most liquids, because much of the heat goes into breaking hydrogen bonds. So the same heat warms water less.

questions.q: Uracil in RNA differs from thymine in DNA in that uracil lacks a:
questions.x: Thymine is uracil with an extra methyl (–CH3) group. Both are single-ringed pyrimidines containing nitrogen.

questions.q: The tertiary structure of a protein is:
o: The order of amino acids in the chain
The arrangement of several polypeptide chains together
The regular coiling of the backbone into a helix
The overall three-dimensional folding of a single polypeptide chain
questions.x: Tertiary structure is how the whole chain, with its helices and sheets, folds into a specific 3-D shape. Several chains together make quaternary structure.

questions.q: Which statement about the bonds in a DNA molecule is correct?
o: Covalent bonds hold each strand together; hydrogen bonds hold the two strands together
Hydrogen bonds hold each strand together; covalent bonds join the two strands
Ionic bonds join the bases across the two strands
Peptide bonds join the nucleotides in each strand
questions.x: Within a strand, nucleotides are joined by covalent phosphodiester bonds. The two strands are held to each other by hydrogen bonds between paired bases.

questions.q: The pyrimidine bases of DNA are:
questions.x: Cytosine and thymine are the single-ringed pyrimidines of DNA. Adenine and guanine are purines, and uracil occurs only in RNA.

questions.q: Which statement about biological macromolecules is correct?
o: They are always freely soluble in water
They have high molecular masses and are built from many monomer units
They contain only carbon and hydrogen
They pass easily through cell membranes
questions.x: Macromolecules such as proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides are large polymers of many monomers. Many, like cellulose, are insoluble, they contain other elements such as oxygen and nitrogen, and their size stops them crossing membranes freely.

questions.q: Which monosaccharide, found in fruits and honey, is the sweetest of the common sugars?
questions.x: Fructose (fruit sugar) is a ketohexose found in fruits and honey and is sweeter than glucose or sucrose.

questions.q: Water forms rounded droplets on a waxy leaf instead of spreading out. This is because:
o: Adhesion of water to the wax is stronger than cohesion between water molecules
Cohesion between water molecules is stronger than their adhesion to the wax
Water reacts chemically with the wax
Water is non-polar, like the wax
questions.x: Wax is non-polar, so water is only weakly attracted to it. The stronger cohesion between water molecules pulls them together into droplets.

questions.q: Cells are treated with an enzyme that digests only proteins, removing all their surface proteins. Carbohydrate chains are still found on the outer surface of the membrane. These chains must belong to:
questions.x: Digesting the proteins removes glycoproteins together with their sugar chains. The remaining surface carbohydrate must be attached to lipids, that is, to glycolipids.

questions.q: Antibiotics such as streptomycin and tetracycline stop protein synthesis in bacteria but do much less harm to human cells. This is because they act on:
o: Peptidoglycan, which is absent from human cells
Mitochondria, which bacteria have in large numbers
70S ribosomes, which differ from the 80S ribosomes in human cytoplasm
questions.x: These drugs bind to bacterial 70S ribosomes. Human cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S, so most human protein synthesis is unaffected. Penicillin, not these drugs, acts on peptidoglycan.

questions.q: During cell division, the nucleolus:
o: Disappears in prophase and reappears in telophase
questions.x: The nucleolus breaks down in early prophase and is formed again at the nucleolar organiser regions in telophase, when the nuclei re-form.

questions.q: Immediately after the centromeres split at anaphase of mitosis, a human cell contains a total of:
questions.x: Each of the 46 chromosomes separates into two chromatids, and each chromatid now counts as a chromosome, so there are 92 until the cell divides.

questions.q: A cell under the microscope has a nucleus, a pair of centrioles, small vacuoles and glycogen granules, but no cell wall. It is most likely:
o: A cell of a flowering plant
questions.x: Centrioles, glycogen and the lack of a wall point to an animal cell. A nucleus rules out bacteria and cyanobacteria.

questions.q: Telomeres become slightly shorter each time a normal body cell divides. This is linked with:
o: Ageing and the limited number of divisions of a cell
questions.x: Each round of DNA replication leaves the chromosome ends a little shorter; when telomeres become too short the cell stops dividing, which is linked with ageing.

questions.q: Oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus but released from the posterior pituitary. It reaches the posterior pituitary by:
o: Being carried in the blood of the general circulation
Travelling down the axons of neurosecretory cells
questions.x: Neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus send their axons down the pituitary stalk, and hormones such as oxytocin travel along them to be stored and released. This is a nervous link, not a general blood route.

questions.q: The medulla oblongata leaves the skull and continues as the spinal cord through the:
questions.x: The foramen magnum is the large opening in the base of the skull where the medulla becomes the spinal cord. The central sulcus and longitudinal fissure are grooves of the cerebrum.

questions.q: A man's eyes and optic nerves are healthy, but after an injury to the back of his cerebrum he cannot see. The damaged part is the:
questions.x: Visual impulses are interpreted in the visual area of the occipital lobe at the back of the cerebrum. If it is damaged, the person cannot see even though the eyes work.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly shows the path from a stimulus to a response?
o: Stimulus → effector → motor neuron → CNS → sensory neuron → receptor
Stimulus → sensory neuron → receptor → CNS → effector → motor neuron
Stimulus → CNS → receptor → motor neuron → sensory neuron → effector
Stimulus → receptor → sensory neuron → CNS → motor neuron → effector
questions.x: The receptor detects the stimulus first and sends impulses along a sensory neuron to the CNS. A motor neuron then carries impulses to the effector.

questions.q: Keeping balance while riding a bicycle and making the movements smooth depend mainly on the:
questions.x: The cerebellum coordinates muscle activity, keeping movements smooth and the body balanced. The hypothalamus regulates internal conditions such as temperature.

questions.q: After training was complete, the sound of the bell in Pavlov's work with dogs served as the:
questions.x: The bell produces salivation only after it has been repeatedly paired with food, so it is a conditioned stimulus. Food is the unconditioned stimulus, and salivation to the bell is the conditioned response.

questions.q: The process of a neuron that carries impulses away from the cell body is the:
questions.x: The axon conducts impulses away from the cell body. Dendrites carry them towards it; Nissl's granules and neurofibrils are structures inside the cytoplasm.

questions.q: Sensory receptors in the body are built in different ways. Which description of their build is accurate?
o: All receptors are free nerve endings without any covering
Some are free nerve endings, while others are specialised cells or capsules linked to nerve endings
All receptors are separate cells with no contact with neurons
Receptors are found only in the special sense organs
questions.x: Pain receptors are free nerve endings, Pacinian corpuscles are capsules around a nerve ending, and taste or rod cells are specialised cells that pass signals to neurons. Receptors also occur in skin, muscles and blood vessels.

questions.q: One enzyme sample is moved slightly away from its optimum pH, and another is put in a very strong acid. Which description of the outcome is right?
o: Any change of pH from the optimum denatures the enzyme permanently
pH has no effect on enzymes
A small change from the optimum always increases activity
A small change from the optimum lowers activity reversibly, but extreme pH denatures the enzyme
questions.x: Slight pH changes alter charges and reduce activity, and returning to the optimum restores it. Extreme pH breaks the bonds holding the enzyme's shape, causing denaturation.

questions.q: In an investigation of the effect of temperature on amylase, which factors must be kept the same in every tube?
o: pH and the concentrations of enzyme and starch
Only the volume of iodine used
No factors need to be kept the same
questions.x: Only temperature should vary; pH, enzyme and substrate concentrations are kept constant so that any change in rate is due to temperature alone.

questions.q: Increasing the concentration of an inhibitor, with other conditions unchanged, usually:
o: Turns the inhibitor into an activator
questions.x: More inhibitor molecules bind more enzyme molecules, so the reaction slows further.

questions.q: On an energy graph of a reaction, the activation energy is shown by the:
o: Difference between the energy of the reactants and the products
Difference between the energy of the reactants and the top of the curve
questions.x: Activation energy is the energy barrier: the rise from the reactants' energy to the peak. The difference between reactants and products is the energy released or absorbed.

questions.q: An enzyme catalyses the reversible reaction A ⇌ B. The enzyme lowers the activation energy of:
o: Both the forward and the reverse reaction
Neither reaction, but raises the product's energy
questions.x: The energy barrier between the two compounds is the same peak approached from either side, so lowering it speeds up both directions.

questions.q: According to the heterotroph hypothesis, the first organisms obtained their energy by:
o: Fermenting organic molecules taken from their surroundings
questions.x: The first cells were heterotrophs living in an organic-rich sea without free oxygen, so they broke down organic molecules anaerobically, as in fermentation.

questions.q: Beetle P lives 2 years and leaves 10 offspring that survive to breed. Beetle Q lives 4 years and leaves 6 such offspring. In Darwinian terms:
o: Beetle P is fitter because it leaves more fertile offspring
Beetle Q is fitter because it lives longer
Both are equally fit because both reproduce
Neither is fit because both eventually die
questions.x: Darwinian fitness is measured by the number of surviving, fertile offspring left, not by lifespan or strength. P leaves 10 against Q's 6.

questions.q: An important gap shared by the theories of both Lamarck and Darwin was that neither could explain:
o: How characters are actually passed from parents to offspring
Why organisms are suited to their surroundings
Why fossils are found in rocks
questions.x: Both lived before genetics was understood, so neither knew how traits are inherited. Mendel's work and later genetics filled this gap.

questions.q: Menstrual bleeding usually lasts about:
questions.x: The menstrual phase normally lasts about 3 to 5 days, at the start of the cycle.

questions.q: A home pregnancy test works by detecting which hormone in a woman's urine?
questions.x: Pregnancy tests detect human chorionic gonadotrophin, which is made only by the embryo and placenta, so its presence indicates pregnancy.

questions.q: Besides sexual contact, HIV is commonly spread by:
o: Shaking hands with an infected person
Sharing needles and transfusion of unscreened blood
questions.x: HIV spreads through blood, semen, vaginal fluid and breast milk, so shared needles and unscreened blood are major routes. Casual contact does not spread it.

questions.q: A whole myofibril shortens noticeably during contraction because:
o: Only the sarcomere at one end shortens greatly
Its thick filaments fold in half
New sarcomeres are removed during contraction
All the sarcomeres along it shorten at the same time
questions.x: A myofibril is a chain of sarcomeres, and they all shorten together, so their small changes add up to a large shortening. Filaments do not fold and sarcomeres are not removed.

questions.q: The knuckle joints, between the metacarpals and the first phalanges of the fingers, are:
questions.x: At the knuckles, the rounded head of a metacarpal fits an oval hollow on the phalanx, allowing bending and side-to-side movement: a condyloid joint. The joints between the phalanges themselves are hinge joints.

questions.q: A footballer had a serious knee injury, with torn cartilage, several years ago. In later life that knee is at higher risk of:
questions.x: Damage to a joint's cartilage speeds up its wear, so an old injury is a known risk factor for osteoarthritis in that joint. Gout and rheumatoid arthritis are caused by uric acid and autoimmunity, not injury.

questions.q: The muscles of facial expression, used in smiling, are:
questions.x: We smile at will, so facial muscles are voluntary skeletal muscles. Involuntary striated muscle describes cardiac muscle.

questions.q: Rheumatoid arthritis is called an autoimmune disease. This means that:
o: It is caused by a virus that attacks immune cells
It spreads from person to person by contact
The joints lose all their immune cells
The body's immune system attacks its own tissues
questions.x: In an autoimmune disease the immune system wrongly attacks the body's own tissue; in rheumatoid arthritis this is mainly the synovial membrane. It is not infectious and is not caused by loss of immune cells.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a type of cell found in bone?
questions.x: Chondroblasts make cartilage. Bone contains osteoblasts (build matrix), osteocytes (maintain it) and osteoclasts (break it down).

questions.q: Arthritis differs from a sprain because arthritis is:
o: A torn ligament, while a sprain is inflammation of cartilage
A broken bone near a joint, while a sprain is a muscle cramp
Inflammation of the joint itself, while a sprain is a stretched or torn ligament
Always caused by injury, while a sprain has no cause
questions.x: Arthritis is inflammation of a joint, from causes such as wear, autoimmunity or crystals. A sprain is an injury in which a ligament is stretched or torn.

questions.q: Which list contains ONLY involuntary muscles?
o: Eyeball muscles, stomach wall, heart wall
questions.x: Cardiac muscle of the heart and smooth muscle of the iris and stomach are all involuntary. The diaphragm, tongue, biceps and eyeball muscles are skeletal (voluntary).

questions.q: Drosophila is suitable for genetic studies for all of the following reasons EXCEPT that it:
o: Has a very large number of chromosomes
Has a short life cycle of about two weeks
Produces many offspring from each cross
Is small and easy to culture in the laboratory
questions.x: Drosophila has only four pairs of chromosomes, which makes its genetics easier to follow. Its short life cycle, many offspring and easy culture are real advantages.

questions.q: Y-linked (holandric) traits never appear in females because females:
o: Have two X chromosomes that mask them
Carry only recessive alleles of these genes
questions.x: Holandric genes are found only on the Y chromosome. Females are XX, so they cannot carry or show these traits.

questions.q: A girl is red–green colour-blind. From whom did she receive the colour-blindness alleles?
o: One from her father and one from her mother
One from her mother and one from a grandparent directly
questions.x: She needs the allele on both X chromosomes, and she received one X from each parent. So her father is colour-blind and her mother at least a carrier.

questions.q: A dominant allele is one that:
o: Is expressed only when two copies are present
Is always more common in a population
Expresses its effect even in the heterozygous condition
Always mutates into the recessive allele
questions.x: A dominant allele shows its effect in the heterozygote (Tt looks like TT). Needing two copies to be expressed describes a recessive allele; dominance says nothing about how common an allele is.

questions.q: Incomplete linkage means that linked genes:
o: Are usually inherited together but are occasionally separated by crossing over
questions.x: In incomplete linkage, crossing over sometimes separates the linked genes, giving a few recombinants. Genes that are never separated show complete linkage.

questions.q: A child has blood group O and the mother has blood group A. Which blood group is NOT possible for the father?
questions.x: A group O child is ii, so the father must pass on an i allele. A group AB father (IᴬIᴮ) has no i allele. A father of group A can be Iᴬi, a father of group B can be Iᴮi, and a group O father is ii.

questions.q: The term 'genotype' means:
o: The visible form of a character
The set of alleles an organism carries for a character
The number of chromosomes in a gamete
The effect of the environment on a trait
questions.x: Genotype is the genetic make-up, for example TT, Tt or tt. The visible form of the character (tall or dwarf) is the phenotype.

questions.q: In a trihybrid cross AaBbCc × AaBbCc with three independent genes, how many different genotypes can occur among the offspring?
questions.x: Each gene gives three genotypes (for example AA, Aa, aa), so three independent genes give 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 different genotypes. 64 is the number of gamete combinations (Punnett boxes) and 8 the number of gamete types per parent.

questions.q: The centre in the brain that adjusts the heart rate through nerves is located in the:
questions.x: The cardiac (cardiovascular) centre is in the medulla oblongata. It sends sympathetic and vagus impulses to speed up or slow down the heart.

questions.q: The chambers of the human heart that receive blood returning in the veins are the:
questions.x: The two atria are the receiving chambers: veins empty into them. The ventricles are the pumping chambers that send blood into the arteries.

questions.q: Within a lymph node, bacteria are engulfed and digested mainly by:
questions.x: Macrophages in the lymph nodes are phagocytes that engulf bacteria and debris filtered from the lymph. Red cells and platelets do not.

questions.q: Water re-enters the blood near the venule end of a capillary bed mainly because there:
o: Blood pressure is greater than at the arteriole end
The osmotic pull of plasma proteins is greater than the blood pressure
Valves in the capillary push the water back
The capillary wall becomes impermeable to water
questions.x: Blood pressure falls along the capillary while the osmotic pressure of plasma proteins stays about the same. Near the venule end osmosis wins and water moves back in.

questions.q: Out of each 0.8-second heartbeat, the contraction of the atria takes about:
questions.x: Of the 0.8 second cycle, atrial systole takes about 0.1 second, ventricular systole about 0.3 second and complete diastole about 0.4 second.

questions.q: After a kidney transplant, a patient takes drugs that suppress the immune system. An expected side effect is:
o: Faster rejection of the new kidney
questions.x: The drugs reduce rejection by weakening the T-cell response, but this also weakens defence against pathogens, so infections become more likely.

questions.q: The injected (Salk) polio vaccine contains:
questions.x: The Salk vaccine uses inactivated virus and is given by injection. The oral Sabin vaccine uses live weakened virus.

questions.q: On the steep middle part of the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve, a small fall in oxygen partial pressure causes:
o: Almost no change in haemoglobin saturation
Haemoglobin to take up more oxygen
A large release of oxygen from haemoglobin
Haemoglobin to bind carbon monoxide instead
questions.x: The steep part of the curve covers the pO₂ found in respiring tissues, so a small drop in pO₂ there makes haemoglobin give up a lot of oxygen. On the flat upper part, small changes have little effect.

questions.q: At the very end of a quiet inspiration, just before expiration begins, the air pressure inside the alveoli is:
o: Lowest of the whole breathing cycle
questions.x: Air flows in only while alveolar pressure is below atmospheric pressure. At the end of inspiration air flow stops, which means the two pressures have become equal. The lowest pressure occurs during inspiration, not at its end.

questions.q: Studies show that the lung cancer death rate of people who give up smoking falls steadily over the following years. This finding supports the idea that:
o: Continued smoking is a cause of lung cancer
Lung cancer is caused by a virus spread between people
questions.x: If removing the exposure lowers the risk, the exposure is likely to be a cause. This evidence, along with the dose-related rise in risk, links smoking causally to lung cancer.

questions.q: The left lung is slightly smaller than the right lung mainly because:
o: The liver pushes up beneath it
It has a hollow (cardiac notch) that makes room for the heart
It receives no branch of the pulmonary artery
Its alveoli are smaller than those of the right lung
questions.x: The heart lies slightly to the left in the thorax, so the left lung has a cardiac notch and only two lobes. The liver lies under the right side, and both lungs receive a pulmonary artery.

questions.q: The roof of the mouth, which separates the oral cavity from the nasal cavity, is formed by the:
o: Soft palate in front and hard palate behind
Hard palate in front and soft palate behind
Hard palate alone, made entirely of bone
questions.x: The palate forms the roof of the mouth: the bony hard palate in front and the muscular soft palate, ending in the uvula, behind. It lets a person chew and breathe at the same time.

questions.q: The dental formula of an adult human shows that each half of the upper jaw contains:
questions.x: Each half jaw of an adult has 2 incisors, 1 canine, 2 premolars and 3 molars, which is 8 teeth. Eight teeth in each of the four half jaws gives the full set of 32.

questions.q: Which capillary bed lies inside Bowman's capsule?
questions.x: The glomerulus is the knot of capillaries enclosed by Bowman's capsule. Peritubular capillaries and vasa recta lie outside, around the tubules.

questions.q: If core body temperature fell well below normal, a direct result would be that:
o: Enzyme-controlled reactions slow down, so metabolism slows
questions.x: At low temperature enzymes are not denatured but work slowly, so all metabolic processes, including those of nerves and heart, slow down. This is why constant temperature is needed.

questions.q: A kidney stone blocks a ureter, and pressure builds up in the tubules and Bowman's capsules of that kidney. Glomerular filtration in that kidney will:
o: Rise, because the capsule pressure helps push fluid in
Stay the same, because filtration depends only on blood pressure
Fall, because the back-pressure in the capsule opposes filtration
Rise, because more water is reabsorbed
questions.x: Fluid pressure in Bowman's capsule pushes back against filtration. When urine cannot drain this pressure rises, the net filtration pressure falls and less filtrate forms.

questions.q: Which statement about blood leaving the glomerulus is correct?
o: Most of its plasma is still in it; only part has been filtered
All of its plasma has been filtered out
It has lost its plasma proteins into the filtrate
It has gained urea from the filtrate
questions.x: Only a fraction, roughly a fifth, of the plasma entering a glomerulus is filtered. The rest, with the cells and proteins, flows on through the efferent arteriole.

questions.q: If the efferent arteriole of a nephron constricts, what happens to the hydrostatic pressure in the peritubular capillaries beyond it?
o: It rises, because more blood is forced into them
It stays the same, as the two beds are not connected
It falls, because more resistance lies before them
It becomes higher than in the glomerulus
questions.x: Narrowing the efferent arteriole raises pressure upstream, in the glomerulus, but blood reaches the peritubular capillaries after passing more resistance, so their pressure falls further.

questions.q: The part of the hypothalamus that starts sweating and dilation of skin arterioles when the blood becomes too warm is the:
questions.x: The heat-loss centre triggers cooling responses; the heat-gain centre triggers shivering and vasoconstriction.

questions.q: The heat that keeps a resting human warm comes mainly from:
o: Friction of blood against vessel walls
Metabolic reactions such as respiration in the liver and muscles
Digestion of cellulose by gut bacteria
questions.x: Humans are endotherms: their heat is produced inside the body by metabolism, especially respiration in active organs like the liver and muscles.

questions.q: A person whose blood calcium is normal is told she has formed a kidney stone. Which explanation is correct?
o: Stones can form with normal blood calcium if the urine is very concentrated
Stones form only when blood calcium is above normal
Stones form only in people who have gout
Stones form only inside the urinary bladder
questions.x: Stone formation depends on the concentration of salts in urine, so low urine volume alone can cause it. Gout and high blood calcium are risk factors, not requirements.

questions.q: Urine moves down the ureters to the bladder mainly by:
o: Peristaltic contractions of the smooth muscle in their walls
The beating of cilia lining the ureters
questions.x: Waves of smooth-muscle contraction (peristalsis) push urine along each ureter. That is why urine still reaches the bladder when a person is lying down.

questions.q: Viruses used in traditional live attenuated vaccines are usually weakened by:
o: Treating them with formaldehyde until they are dead
Growing them repeatedly in cell cultures or animals until they lose their virulence
Mixing them with antibodies from a recovered patient
questions.x: Repeated growth in culture selects variants that multiply well in the laboratory but cause little or no disease in humans. Formaldehyde treatment kills the virus, which gives an inactivated vaccine, not an attenuated one.

questions.q: After a radioactively labelled probe has hybridised with DNA on a membrane, its position is usually revealed by:
o: Placing the membrane against X-ray film (autoradiography)
Examining it under a light microscope only
questions.x: Radiation from the bound probe darkens photographic or X-ray film, showing bands where the target sequence is. Fluorescent probes are seen under suitable light instead.

questions.q: After vaccination, the antibodies themselves are secreted by:
o: Plasma cells developed from B lymphocytes
questions.x: Antigen in the vaccine activates B lymphocytes, which divide and form plasma cells that secrete antibodies, as well as memory B cells. Neutrophils engulf microbes but do not make antibodies.

questions.q: Iron rusts according to 4Fe + 3O₂ → 2Fe₂O₃. How many moles of iron are needed to form 1 mol of Fe₂O₃?
questions.x: The ratio Fe : Fe₂O₃ is 4 : 2 = 2 : 1, so 1 mol of Fe₂O₃ needs 2 mol of Fe. This also matches the two Fe atoms in each formula unit.

questions.q: A student says, 'The reactant with the smaller mass is always the limiting reactant.' This is wrong because the limiting reactant depends on:
o: The number of moles present and the mole ratio in the equation
The order in which the reactants are mixed
Which reactant has the larger molar mass
The temperature at which the reaction is done
questions.x: Equal masses of different substances contain different numbers of moles, and the equation may need them in unequal amounts. Only moles compared with the mole ratio decide which runs out first.

questions.q: Sulphur burns as S + O₂ → SO₂. 16 g of sulphur burnt in excess air gives 24 g of SO₂. What is the percentage yield? (S = 32, O = 16)
questions.x: S = 16/32 = 0.5 mol, so the theoretical SO₂ = 0.5 × 64 = 32 g. Yield = 24/32 × 100 = 75%. 150% wrongly compares 24 g with the 16 g of sulphur.

questions.q: Goldstein could observe positive rays in his tube only under conditions of:
o: High gas pressure and low voltage
Low gas pressure and high voltage
High gas pressure and high voltage
Normal air pressure and no voltage
questions.x: At low pressure and high voltage, cathode-ray electrons strike gas molecules and ionise them; the positive ions then stream towards the cathode.

questions.q: Goldstein gave which other name to the rays he saw passing through the holes of a perforated cathode?
questions.x: Goldstein called them canal rays because they pass through the holes (canals) of a perforated cathode. Cathode rays are streams of electrons, not positive particles.

questions.q: The charge on a proton is:
questions.x: A proton carries a positive charge of 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, equal in size to the electron's charge. The values 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ and 1.673 × 10⁻²⁷ are masses in kg, not charges.

questions.q: At 25 °C, the molecules of which gas have the lowest average speed? (H 1, He 4, C 12, N 14, Cl 35.5)
questions.x: At the same temperature all molecules have the same average kinetic energy, so the heaviest molecules move slowest. Cl₂ (M = 71) is the heaviest here.

questions.q: A gas has a density of 1.25 g dm⁻³ at STP. Its molar mass is about:
questions.x: Molar mass = density × molar volume = 1.25 × 22.4 = 28 g mol⁻¹. Dividing 22.4 by 1.25 instead gives the wrong 17.9.

questions.q: A mixture of 0.5 mol of O₂ and 0.5 mol of N₂ behaves ideally. What volume does it occupy at STP?
questions.x: Volume at STP depends only on the total number of moles: 0.5 + 0.5 = 1 mol, which occupies 22.4 dm³. The kind of gas does not matter.

questions.q: Which liquid has dipole–dipole attractions between its molecules but NO hydrogen bonding?
questions.x: Propanone is polar (C=O) but has no H bonded to O, N or F, so its molecules attract by dipole–dipole forces only. Methanol and water hydrogen-bond; hexane is non-polar.

questions.q: In a body-centred cubic arrangement, metal atoms sit at every corner and one sits in the middle of the cube. The effective number of atoms per cell is:
questions.x: Each corner atom is shared by 8 cells: 8 × 1/8 = 1, plus 1 atom wholly inside, giving 2. Counting 9 ignores sharing.

questions.q: A small, highly charged cation distorts the electron cloud of a large anion, giving the bond some covalent character and changing the crystal structure. This effect is called:
questions.x: Distortion of an anion's electron cloud by a cation is polarisation. It is one reason structures can differ from simple radius-ratio predictions.

questions.q: CaCO₃ heated in an open vessel decomposes completely, but in a closed vessel it reaches equilibrium. The reason is that in the closed vessel:
o: CO₂ cannot escape, so it recombines with CaO
The temperature cannot rise high enough
No CO₂ is formed at all
questions.x: CaCO₃ ⇌ CaO + CO₂. In an open vessel CO₂ escapes, so the reverse reaction cannot occur; in a closed vessel it stays and re-forms CaCO₃.

questions.q: If the Haber process were run at 700 °C instead of about 450 °C, the result would be:
o: A slower rate and a lower equilibrium yield
A faster rate and a higher equilibrium yield
A slower rate but a higher equilibrium yield
A faster rate but a lower equilibrium yield of ammonia
questions.x: A higher temperature always speeds up the reaction, but the forward reaction is exothermic, so the equilibrium shifts left and less ammonia is present.

questions.q: Removing ammonia from the equilibrium mixture N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ causes:
o: The equilibrium to shift to the left
More N₂ and H₂ to combine, as the equilibrium shifts to the right
No change in the amounts of N₂ and H₂
questions.x: Removing a product makes the system replace it, so more N₂ and H₂ react. Kc stays the same at constant temperature.

questions.q: The energy profile of a two-step reaction shows two humps; the first hump is much higher than the second. Which statement is correct?
o: The second step is rate-determining because it comes last
Both steps proceed at the same rate, so neither controls the rate
The first step is rate-determining because it has the higher activation energy
The intermediate is located at the highest point of the profile
questions.x: The step with the larger barrier is slower and controls the overall rate. The intermediate lies in the dip between the two humps, not at a peak.

questions.q: In the Contact process, traces of arsenic compounds reduce the activity of the platinum catalyst. The catalysed reaction slows down because the arsenic:
o: Raises the temperature of the catalyst
Increases the enthalpy change of the reaction
Blocks the active sites, so the low-activation-energy pathway is no longer available
Reacts with SO₃ to reverse the reaction
questions.x: Arsenic acts as a catalytic poison: it occupies the catalyst surface, so the reaction must follow the uncatalysed, higher-Ea route.

questions.q: According to the first law of thermodynamics, the total energy of the universe:
questions.x: System plus surroundings make up the universe. Energy lost by one is gained by the other, so the total energy stays constant.

questions.q: Which of these equations describes a change that takes in heat from its surroundings?
questions.x: Splitting water into its elements is the reverse of the strongly exothermic burning of hydrogen, so it absorbs heat. Combustion and neutralisation give out heat.

questions.q: Water in an open dish slowly evaporates at room temperature. This process is:
questions.x: Evaporation happens by itself, yet it takes in heat (it is endothermic). So a negative ΔH is not essential for a change to be spontaneous.

questions.q: When magnesium burns in oxygen, 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO, the species that gains electrons is:
questions.x: Each oxygen atom gains two electrons to become O²⁻, so oxygen is reduced while magnesium loses electrons and is oxidised.

questions.q: When methane burns, CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, the oxidation number of carbon changes from:
questions.x: In CH₄, x + 4(+1) = 0 gives −4; in CO₂, x + 2(−2) = 0 gives +4. Carbon is oxidised.

questions.q: Which molecule contains carbon atoms with all three types of hybridisation, sp³, sp² and sp?
questions.x: In CH₃–CH=CH–C≡CH the CH₃ carbon is sp³, the two C=C carbons are sp² and the two C≡C carbons are sp. Each of the other molecules lacks one of these types.

questions.q: The C–Cl bond is polar, but the Cl–Cl bond is not. The reason is that:
o: The C–Cl bond is a double bond
Chlorine is more electronegative than carbon, while the two atoms in Cl₂ are identical
Carbon is more electronegative than chlorine
questions.x: In Cl–Cl both atoms attract the shared pair equally, so there is no ionic character. In C–Cl the more electronegative chlorine pulls the pair towards itself.

questions.q: The nitrogen molecule, N≡N, contains:
o: Two sigma and one pi bond
One sigma and two pi bonds
questions.x: A triple bond is made of one σ bond (head-on overlap) and two π bonds (sideways overlap of two pairs of p orbitals).

questions.q: Sodium peroxide reacts with carbon dioxide: 2Na₂O₂ + 2CO₂ → 2Na₂CO₃ + O₂. In this reaction the oxygen of the peroxide ion is:
questions.x: Peroxide oxygen is −1. Some becomes −2 (in Na₂CO₃, reduced) and some becomes 0 (in O₂, oxidised), so it disproportionates.

questions.q: The hydroxides formed when alkali metals react with water become stronger bases down the group. Which is the strongest base?
questions.x: Down Group I the M–OH bond becomes more ionic as the cation gets larger, so CsOH releases OH⁻ most readily and is the strongest base.

questions.q: Iron has atomic number 26. Its ground-state electronic configuration is:
questions.x: After argon (18 electrons), the 4s orbital takes 2 and the 3d subshell takes the remaining 6. Iron has no special half-filled or filled d arrangement, so it is 3d⁶ 4s².

questions.q: Propene, CH₃CH=CH₂, is classified as:
questions.x: Propene has no ring, so it is open-chain, and its C=C double bond makes it unsaturated.

questions.q: 9.2 g of methylbenzene (C₇H₈, M = 92 g mol⁻¹) is hydrogenated completely to methylcyclohexane. What volume of hydrogen at STP is used?
questions.x: Moles of methylbenzene = 9.2/92 = 0.1. It needs 3 mol H₂ per mole, so 0.3 mol × 22.4 = 6.72 dm³.

questions.q: The carbon–carbon bond length in benzene is about:
questions.x: All C–C bonds in benzene are about 1.39 Å, between the single-bond length (1.54 Å) and the double-bond length (1.34 Å). 1.20 Å is the C≡C length.

questions.q: Which step restores the aromatic character of the ring in electrophilic substitution?
o: Formation of the electrophile from the reagent and catalyst
Attack of the electrophile on the π electrons
Addition of a nucleophile to the arenium ion
Loss of H⁺ from the arenium ion
questions.x: When the sp³ carbon loses its H⁺, the two electrons of the C–H bond return to the ring, which regains its six delocalised π electrons.

questions.q: For bonding, an ethene carbon has available:
o: Three sp² hybrid orbitals and one unhybridised p orbital
Two sp hybrid orbitals and two unhybridised p orbitals
Three sp² hybrid orbitals and no unhybridised p orbital
questions.x: Mixing one 2s and two 2p orbitals gives three sp² orbitals for the σ bonds. The remaining 2p orbital on each carbon forms the π bond.

questions.q: When naming a branched alkane by the IUPAC system, the parent chain chosen is:
o: The longest continuous chain of carbon atoms
The chain with the most branches written on the left
Any chain that is written in a straight line
The shortest chain that contains all the branches
questions.x: The parent name comes from the longest continuous carbon chain, however it is drawn. Branches are then numbered from the end that gives them the lowest locants.

questions.q: The nitration of benzene, C₆H₆ + HNO₃ → C₆H₅NO₂ + H₂O (with concentrated H₂SO₄), is an example of:
questions.x: The electrophile NO₂⁺ replaces one ring hydrogen, and the aromatic ring is kept, so it is electrophilic substitution.

questions.q: The IUPAC name of the straight-chain alkane CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃ is:
questions.x: The chain has six carbon atoms joined by single bonds, so it is hexane. Pentane has five carbons and heptane seven.

questions.q: Tertiary alkyl halides react readily by the SN1 mechanism mainly because:
o: The tertiary carbocation is stabilised by electron release from three alkyl groups
The tertiary carbon is the least hindered for backside attack
The nucleophile concentration controls their rate
Tertiary alkyl halides have the strongest C–X bond
questions.x: SN1 depends on forming a carbocation, and the three alkyl groups push electrons towards the positive carbon (+I effect), making it stable. Backside attack belongs to SN2.

questions.q: In the name SN1, the number 1 shows that:
o: The reaction is completed in a single step
Only one species, the alkyl halide, takes part in the rate-determining step
The nucleophile carries a charge of −1
questions.x: The 1 means unimolecular: the slow step involves only RX ionising. SN1 actually takes two steps, so a single step is wrong.

questions.q: Which of the following is a weaker acid than phenol?
questions.x: The –CH₃ group releases electrons, destabilising the phenoxide ion, so 4-methylphenol (p-cresol) is less acidic than phenol. Nitro groups withdraw electrons and make phenols more acidic.

questions.q: Ethanol is heated with excess concentrated sulphuric acid at about 170 °C. The main organic product is:
questions.x: At about 170 °C with excess acid, ethanol is dehydrated (loses H₂O within one molecule) to give ethene. At a lower temperature with excess ethanol, the ether is formed instead.

questions.q: Two molecules of propanal, CH₃CH₂CHO, combine in dilute NaOH. The aldol product is:
questions.x: The base removes an α-H from CH₂, and the carbanion CH₃CH⁻CHO attacks the C=O of a second molecule, giving CH₃CH₂CH(OH)CH(CH₃)CHO: 3-hydroxy-2-methylpentanal. 3-Hydroxybutanal is the aldol from ethanal.

questions.q: In acid-catalysed nucleophilic addition to a carbonyl compound, H⁺ speeds up the reaction because protonating the oxygen:
o: Turns the nucleophile into a stronger base
Makes the carbonyl carbon more positive and so more easily attacked by weak nucleophiles
Removes the α-hydrogen from the molecule
questions.x: When the oxygen is protonated, the positive charge is shared with the carbonyl carbon, which becomes much more electrophilic. Even weak nucleophiles such as water, alcohols or NH₂OH can then add.

questions.q: Ethanoic acid mixes with water in all proportions mainly because:
o: It has a very high molar mass
It reacts completely with water to form ethanol
Its –COOH group forms hydrogen bonds with water molecules
questions.x: The C=O and O–H of the carboxyl group hydrogen-bond with water, so lower acids are miscible; solubility falls as the hydrocarbon chain grows.

questions.q: Which protein is correctly matched with where it is mainly found?
questions.x: Albumin is the main protein of egg white. Casein is in milk, keratin in hair and nails, and haemoglobin in red blood cells.

questions.q: When nylon-6,6 is made from hexane-1,6-diamine and hexanedioic acid, each amide link formed releases one molecule of:
questions.x: –NH₂ of the diamine and –COOH of the acid join as –CO–NH– and lose H₂O, which is why this is condensation polymerisation. HCl is released only when the acid chloride is used instead.

questions.q: The vector product of a vector P with itself, P × P, is:
questions.x: The angle between P and itself is 0° and sin 0° = 0, so P × P is the null vector. P² is the scalar product P · P.

questions.q: A 2 kg shell moving at 10 m s⁻¹ explodes into pieces of 1.5 kg and 0.5 kg. The 0.5 kg piece moves backward at 20 m s⁻¹. The velocity of the 1.5 kg piece is:
questions.x: Momentum before = 2 × 10 = 20 kg m s⁻¹. After: 1.5v + 0.5 × (−20) = 20, so 1.5v = 30 and v = 20 m s⁻¹ forward.

questions.q: A ball rolls along a straight floor and gradually comes to rest. Its displacement–time graph is:
o: A curve that gets steeper and steeper
A curve that gets flatter and finally becomes horizontal
A horizontal line from the start
questions.x: The slope of the graph is the velocity. As the ball slows down the slope decreases, and when it stops the graph becomes horizontal.

questions.q: Two stones are thrown from level ground with equal speeds and land at the same distance. One was launched at 25° above the horizontal. Ignoring air resistance, the other was launched at:
questions.x: Equal ranges at the same speed occur for complementary angles, θ and 90° − θ, because sin 2θ is the same for both. 90° − 25° = 65°.

questions.q: For a body moving with uniform acceleration, the acceleration–time graph is:
o: A straight line sloping upward through the origin
questions.x: Uniform acceleration means a has the same value at every instant, so a plotted against t gives a horizontal line.

questions.q: A cyclist moving in one direction along a straight road covers the first half of the distance at 20 m s⁻¹ and the second half at 30 m s⁻¹. Her average velocity is:
questions.x: For equal distances, v̄ = 2v₁v₂/(v₁ + v₂) = 2 × 20 × 30 ÷ 50 = 24 m s⁻¹. 25 m s⁻¹ would be correct only for equal times.

questions.q: A car drives 8 km due north and then 6 km due south along the same road. The distance covered and the displacement are:
questions.x: Distance adds up the path: 8 + 6 = 14 km. Displacement is the net change in position: 8 − 6 = 2 km, still north of the start.

questions.q: The kilowatt-hour, printed on electricity bills, is a unit of:
questions.x: A kilowatt-hour is power multiplied by time (1 kW for 1 h), so it is a unit of energy, equal to 3.6 × 10⁶ J.

questions.q: Kinetic energy is the energy a body possesses because of its:
questions.x: Kinetic energy is energy due to motion, ½mv². Energy due to position or shape is potential energy.

questions.q: A 5 kg box is pushed 6 m at constant speed across a level floor. The coefficient of friction is 0.2. The heat produced by friction is (g = 10 m s⁻²):
questions.x: Friction = μmg = 0.2 × 5 × 10 = 10 N. Heat = work against friction = 10 × 6 = 60 J. Using mg × d = 300 J forgets μ.

questions.q: A body moves uniformly in a circle with time period T. Its angular speed is:
questions.x: In one period the body turns through 2π rad, so ω = 2π/T.

questions.q: A gas in steady flow passes from a pipe section of area 2S into a section of area S. Its density rises from ρ to 2ρ. If its speed in the wide section is v, its speed in the narrow section is:
questions.x: Mass flow is conserved: ρ × 2S × v = 2ρ × S × v₂, so v₂ = v. Ignoring the density change and using Av = constant gives the wrong answer 2v.

questions.q: Bernoulli's equation does not apply exactly to a real viscous liquid because:
o: Some of the work done by pressure is turned into heat by internal friction, so mechanical energy is not conserved
A viscous liquid has no kinetic energy
Viscous liquids cannot flow through horizontal tubes
Viscosity makes the liquid's density zero
questions.x: The derivation assumes all the work done by pressure goes into kinetic (and potential) energy. Viscous friction dissipates part of it as heat, breaking that energy balance.

questions.q: Which of the following flows is NOT usually turbulent?
o: Very slow flow of oil through a thin tube
Water from a fully opened fire hose
Smoke rising high above a large fire
questions.x: Slow, viscous flow in a thin tube is laminar. Strong wind, a fire-hose jet and smoke high above a fire are fast, irregular flows with eddies.

questions.q: Water flows at 2 m s⁻¹ through a pipe of cross-sectional area 5 × 10⁻⁴ m². How many litres of water flow out in one minute? (1 litre = 10⁻³ m³)
questions.x: Flow rate Av = 5 × 10⁻⁴ × 2 = 10⁻³ m³ s⁻¹ = 1 litre per second, so 60 litres flow in 60 s.

questions.q: The SI unit of frequency, the hertz (Hz), is equivalent to:
questions.x: Frequency is the number of vibrations per second, so 1 Hz = 1 s⁻¹. The second is the unit of time period, which is the reciprocal of frequency.

questions.q: A 1 kg mass on a spring of spring constant 100 N m⁻¹ oscillates with amplitude 0.1 m. Its total energy is:
questions.x: Total energy = ½kx₀² = ½ × 100 × (0.1)² = 0.5 J. Leaving out the ½ gives 1 J.

questions.q: To send a continuous train of waves (not just a single pulse) along a stretched rope, the end of the rope must be:
o: Moved up and down repeatedly at a steady rate
Given one sharp jerk and then held still
questions.x: A continuous wave needs a continuous source of vibration; each up-and-down cycle of the hand sends out one wavelength. A single jerk gives only a pulse.

questions.q: Which of the following motions is NOT simple harmonic?
o: A mass oscillating on a light spring
A simple pendulum swinging through a small angle
The projection on a diameter of a point moving uniformly round a circle
A ball bouncing up and down on a hard floor
questions.x: For SHM the restoring force must be proportional to displacement from a mean position. A bouncing ball feels only its constant weight between impacts, so its motion is periodic but not SHM.

questions.q: A sound wave and a light wave both pass from air into water. Which statement is correct?
o: Sound speeds up, but light slows down
Sound slows down, but light speeds up
questions.x: Sound, a mechanical wave, travels faster in water (about 1500 m s⁻¹) than in air (about 340 m s⁻¹). Light is fastest in a vacuum and slows down in water, which is optically denser than air.

questions.q: A spot on a turntable makes 2 rotations every second, and its shadow on a wall performs SHM. The angular frequency of the shadow's motion is:
questions.x: The angular frequency of the SHM equals the angular velocity of the rotating point: ω = 2πf = 2π × 2 = 4π rad s⁻¹.

questions.q: A beaker holds just 1 g of water (c = 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹). Warming it through 1 K takes:
questions.x: 1 g = 0.001 kg, so Q = 0.001 × 4200 × 1 = 4.2 J. Forgetting to change grams into kilograms gives 4200 J.

questions.q: When you hold a piece of ice, your hand feels cold. This is because:
o: Coldness flows from the ice into your hand
Thermal energy flows from your hand to the ice
Thermal energy flows from the ice to your hand
No energy is transferred between them
questions.x: Your hand is at a higher temperature than the ice, so thermal energy flows out of your hand into the ice; losing heat is what feels cold.

questions.q: The numerical value of Cp − Cv for one mole of any ideal gas equals the gas constant, about:
questions.x: For an ideal gas Cp − Cv = R, the molar gas constant, which is about 8.3 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹.

questions.q: A capacitor is charged through a resistor. For practical purposes it is regarded as fully charged after about:
questions.x: After one time constant it has only 63% of its final charge. After about 5RC it is above 99%, so it is treated as fully charged.

questions.q: Two identical small spheres each carry charge +q and repel with force F at separation r. Half of the charge on one sphere is moved to the other, and the separation is kept at r. The new force is:
questions.x: The charges become q/2 and 3q/2, whose product is 3q²/4 instead of q². Since F ∝ q₁q₂, the force becomes 3F/4, even though the total charge is unchanged.

questions.q: Two identical positive charges sit on a horizontal line. At a spot directly above the point halfway between them (not at that point itself), their combined field points:
o: Vertically downward, towards the line joining the charges
Horizontally, parallel to the line joining the charges
Vertically upward, away from the line joining the charges
Nowhere, since the field is zero at every such spot
questions.x: The horizontal components of the two fields cancel by symmetry; the vertical components add, pointing away from the positive charges, i.e. upward.

questions.q: Electrons drift through a wire at only about a millimetre per second, yet a lamp lights almost the moment it is switched on. This is because:
o: Electrons travel from the switch to the lamp at the speed of light
The lamp stores electrons until it is switched on
Current flows only in the lamp and not in the wires
The electric field is set up throughout the circuit almost instantly, so electrons everywhere start drifting together
questions.x: Switching on sets up the electric field along the whole circuit at nearly the speed of light, so free electrons already in the lamp filament start moving at once.

questions.q: An electron moves vertically downward in a uniform horizontal magnetic field directed towards the north. The magnetic force on the electron is directed towards the:
questions.x: For a positive charge, v (down) × B (north) points east. The electron is negative, so its force is reversed, towards the west.

questions.q: A positive charge moves towards the right across this page in a uniform magnetic field directed into the page. The magnetic force on it is directed:
o: Towards the bottom of the page
Towards the top of the page
questions.x: F = q(v × B). With v to the right and B into the page, v × B points towards the top of the page, and q is positive.

questions.q: A flat loop lies in the plane of this page in a magnetic field directed into the page. The field is decreasing. Seen from the front, the induced current in the loop flows:
o: Not at all, since the field is into the page
questions.x: The induced current must make a field into the page to oppose the decrease. A clockwise current (seen from the front) gives a field into the page.

questions.q: An alternating voltage v = V₀ sin ωt starts from zero at t = 0. At t = T/4, where T is its period, its phase and value are:
o: π, with v back to zero
π/2, with v at its peak value V₀
π/4, with v equal to half of V₀
2π, with v at its negative peak
questions.x: Phase ωt = (2π/T)(T/4) = π/2, and sin(π/2) = 1, so the voltage is at its peak V₀.

questions.q: A half-wave rectifier uses a silicon diode that drops 0.7 V when conducting. If the peak AC input is 12.7 V, the peak voltage across the load is:
questions.x: The diode takes 0.7 V of the forward voltage, so the load receives 12.7 − 0.7 = 12 V at the peak. Adding the drop (13.4 V) or halving the input are common mistakes.

questions.q: Graphs of maximum photoelectron kinetic energy against light frequency are drawn for two metals with different work functions. The two straight lines are:
o: Of different slopes, passing through the same point
Parallel, with different intercepts on the frequency axis
questions.x: Each slope equals h, the same for every metal, so the lines are parallel. Different work functions give different threshold frequencies, hence different intercepts.

questions.q: All the lines of the Balmer series are produced by transitions ending at:
questions.x: Every Balmer line comes from an electron falling from a higher level (n = 3, 4, 5 …) down to n = 2.

questions.q: Isotope P has a larger decay constant than isotope Q. Compared with Q, isotope P has:
o: A shorter half-life and decays faster
A longer half-life and decays faster
A shorter half-life and decays more slowly
The same half-life but more nuclei
questions.x: T½ = 0.693/λ, so a larger λ means a shorter half-life: a greater fraction of P's nuclei decays each second.

questions.q: After two nights of little sleep, Hamza felt lethargic in the morning lectures. He yawned, his eyes kept closing, and when the teacher asked him a question he answered slowly, as if every word were heavy. He did not even feel like walking to the canteen at break. As used in the passage, 'lethargic' means:
questions.x: Yawning, closing eyes, slow answers and no wish to walk all point to having no energy. Lack of sleep, not boredom, is given as the cause.

questions.q: The stray dog had been chased and beaten by boys many times. When Ayesha first knelt down and held out a piece of bread, it was hostile: it backed away, bared its teeth and growled. Only after she had visited it every day for two weeks did it begin to wag its tail when it saw her. As used in the passage, 'hostile' means:
questions.x: Backing away, baring its teeth and growling show an unfriendly, threatening attitude. Its later tail-wagging shows the change from hostility to trust.

questions.q: Which sentence places 'carefully' correctly?
questions.x: An adverb of manner should not come between a verb and its object; it usually goes after the object.

questions.q: Change into the active voice: "The thief was caught by the police."
o: The police have caught the thief.
The police were catching the thief.
questions.x: 'Was caught' is simple past passive, so the active form is the simple past with the agent 'the police' as subject.

questions.q: Choose the correct option: "So tired ___ that she fell asleep at her desk."
questions.x: When 'So + adjective' begins the sentence, the verb 'be' comes before the subject: 'So tired was Ayesha'.

questions.q: Choose the word that best completes the sentence: "It was bitterly cold; ___, we lit a fire."
questions.x: The fire was lit because of the cold, so a result word, 'therefore', is needed.

questions.q: Choose the correct form: "Hamza regrets ___ rude to his teacher yesterday."
questions.x: 'Regret + gerund' refers to something done in the past that one is sorry about.

questions.q: "The new examination hall is so spacious that all five hundred candidates sat comfortably with room to spare." The word 'spacious' means:
questions.x: 'Spacious' means having plenty of room; the clue is that five hundred people sat comfortably with room to spare.

questions.q: Choose the correct version of this sentence: "No sooner did the guests arrive when the lights went out."
o: No sooner had the guests arrived than the lights went out.
No sooner had the guests arrived when the lights went out.
No sooner the guests had arrived than the lights went out.
No sooner did the guests arrived than the lights went out.
questions.x: 'No sooner' is paired with 'than', not 'when', and for one past action before another it takes inverted past perfect: 'No sooner had the guests arrived than...'.

questions.q: A college rule says: "A student who is absent for more than 10 days will not be allowed to sit the exam." Sana was absent for 7 days. Which statement is correct?
o: Sana will certainly be allowed to sit the exam
The rule alone does not tell us whether Sana may sit the exam
Sana will not be allowed to sit the exam
Sana has broken the college rule
questions.x: The rule only says what happens after more than 10 days of absence. It says nothing about students absent for fewer days, so other rules could still apply to Sana.

questions.q: Which statement means exactly the same as "If a number is divisible by 6, it is divisible by 3"?
o: If a number is divisible by 3, it is divisible by 6
If a number is not divisible by 3, it is not divisible by 6
If a number is not divisible by 6, it is not divisible by 3
Some numbers divisible by 6 are not divisible by 3
questions.x: The contrapositive (if not 3, then not 6) always has the same meaning as the original. Reversing it fails: 9 is divisible by 3 but not by 6.

questions.q: Find the next number: 1, 9, 25, 49, ?
questions.x: These are squares of the odd numbers 1, 3, 5, 7. The next odd number is 9, and 9 x 9 = 81.

questions.q: Find the next number: 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, ?
questions.x: Each term is the sum of the two terms before it: 13 + 21 = 34.

questions.q: Saad is the only son of Kamal. Hira is Kamal's daughter. Nazia is Saad's wife, and Ahmed is the son of Saad and Nazia. How is Hira related to Ahmed?
questions.x: Hira and Saad are both Kamal's children, so Hira is Saad's sister. Saad is Ahmed's father, so Hira is Ahmed's father's sister, his paternal aunt.

questions.q: Ali, Hamza and Bilal each have a bicycle of a different colour: red, blue or green. Ali's bicycle is neither red nor blue. Hamza's bicycle is not red. What colour is Bilal's bicycle?
questions.x: Ali's must be green. Hamza's is not red, so it is blue. Bilal's is the one left, red.

questions.q: Statement: Many students in a hostel get stomach infections because the water tank on its roof is never cleaned. Courses of action: I. The tank should be cleaned and covered regularly. II. Students should be advised to drink boiled or filtered water until then. III. The hostel should be shut down. Which course(s) of action follow?
o: I, II and III all follow
questions.x: Cleaning the tank removes the cause, and safe drinking water protects students meanwhile. Shutting the hostel is extreme when the fault can be fixed.

questions.q: Statement: A survey shows that many students of a college do not know how to use the new online admission portal. Courses of action: I. The college should hold help sessions on using the portal. II. The college should stop online admissions altogether. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: Help sessions fill the gap the survey found. Scrapping the portal throws away a useful system because some students need guidance.

questions.q: An iron gate in a coastal town rusts much faster than an identical gate in a dry inland town. What is the most likely cause?
o: The coastal gate is opened less often
Inland gates are painted every week by law
The moist, salty air near the sea speeds up rusting
Iron does not rust in dry towns at all
questions.x: Rusting needs water and oxygen, and salt speeds it up. Coastal air has more moisture and salt, so the gate there rusts faster.
